blocks.text: My Lord, may I call Dr Andrew Brunton to give evidence, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR ANDREW BRUNTON (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Could you state your full name, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: My name is Dr Andrew Brunton.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And your occupation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm a consultant neonatologist.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And where are you currently based?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I work at the Royal Hospital for Children in Glasgow.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And as part of your training, over recent years were you in 2015 based in the Countess of Chester Hospital as a paediatric trainee?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And as of June 2015, what stage had you reached in your training and experience?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was an ST4, or a specialist trainee year 4, in paediatrics.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And would ST4s sometimes be referred to as registrars?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Dr Brunton, I'm going to ask you about your recollection of your involvement with the baby [Baby D] --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- during the course of which I'm going to draw your attention to clinical records that you made and they'll appear on that screen to your right. You may want to move the water vessel, it might be obscuring your view.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We know that you made a statement to the police some time ago in relation to [Baby D] and could you confirm that, prior to doing so, you were given and took the opportunity of refreshing your memory from the contemporaneous clinical notes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: We understand, is it right, that you were on duty at the Countess of Chester Hospital on Saturday, 20 June 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Is it right that you first met [Baby D] at about 9 pm on that Saturday night --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- when you had just started your night shift?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, I wonder whether you could put on screen, please, slide 34.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Brunton, just to familiarise you with the presentation that's on screen now, it's a chronological presentation, you can see your name at a time, 21.45, and if we click behind it a third party has summarised, under the heading here "description", the contents of your clinical notes which we'll now click on to so you can see the original.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: First, on that page is an entry from a colleague, Dr Rylance, but if we scroll down you will no doubt recognise your own handwriting; do you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I do.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. I've been informed a little of the protocols at the Countess of Chester Hospital, but could you confirm that you, having come on duty for the night shift on the Saturday, you would have received some introduction and information about the patients being handed over to your care?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, we would have had a handover. It normally took place in the paediatric ward, but a handover of both the paediatric and the neonatal patients. I can't remember the exact time of it but we would have had a formal handover.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Having received the information from a colleague did you then, as this note suggests, at 21.45, on Saturday 20th, did you go and examine the baby and consider the data generated by the monitoring of [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. 21.45 might be an approximate time, but around that time, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So you would undertake the observations and then note up as you went along or would you do it retrospectively at the end of your examination of the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I would normally write it at the end of examining the baby.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. And if you could then please take us through the notes that you made and help us understand them. So the handover was given by your colleague Dr Rylance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Your first note says "repeat gas". Does that inform the reader that this was a second reading of the baby's gas tests, as it were?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I presume so, that's the first one that's been brought to my attention. But that may have been in the context of from the handover previously, but I can't be certain of that.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Could you take us through the entries there to the right of the colon?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The right of the colon shows that the pH, the acid levels in the blood, were 7.24. PC02, the carbon dioxide level, was 7.49. The base excess was minus 4.6 and the lactate level was 2.7.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: I'm grateful. Let's look at them one by one.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see alongside pH 7.24 what appears to be an arrow pointing upwards.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I'm presuming, I can't remember what the previous gas result was, but the arrow pointing upwards would have indicated, normally in my clinical notes, that that was an improvement.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. What are the pH levels indicative of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The pH levels will measure the acidity level in the blood.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So the arrow pointing upwards from your noting indicates an improvement --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: An improvement, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- rather than an increased level?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. And the next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the carbon dioxide level was 7.49. There's an arrow pointing downwards besides that. Again, I can't remember the previous gas, but my presumption would be that that would be an improvement compared to the previous one.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Could you help me understand that? You seem to have arrows in opposite directions, both indicative of an improvement.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: An improvement clinically. So we've seen that the acid level is improving within the blood, even though the number is going up, that's a good thing, as it means that the acid level is reducing within the blood.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Likewise, the carbon dioxide level, which can sometimes drive the acidity within the blood, is coming down. So those two figures together indicate an improvement.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The base excess was minus 4.6. The base excess is a rough figure that we look at that is used to -- that's helpful in terms of trying to work out whether the gas, if it's abnormal in any way, is being driven by a respiratory perspective or what we call a metabolic perspective, but that number would be within acceptable limits.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So the 4.6 is, all things considered, within acceptable limits?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And the lactate of 2.7?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Lactate of 2.7, again in the context of [Baby D]'s clinical status at that time, would be within acceptable limits.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So exercising your clinical judgment, taking into account those four readings collectively, what was the picture?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, like I say, I would need to see the previous gas to see how that was but from that gas result there is a slight improvement. However, as you can see, I don't know if you want me to go on --
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Yes, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: -- but in the next sentence what I've said is that the baby's currently on non-invasive respiratory support, which means CPAP, which is also defined as continuous positive airway pressure. And the end expiratory pressure, which is what that word PEEP is, is a measure of how much force we are having to give to keep the lungs open. And what we're also looking at after that there is where it says "in 48% O2". That is the amount of oxygen [Baby D] was requiring at that time. So that was a high level of oxygen.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Could you just help us understand why you have used the word "however" (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because the gas shows an improvement but clinically correlating that gas against [Baby D] she had not clinically improved at that time.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: As evidenced by her requirement for the continuing CPAP --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- at those levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and the subsequent observations underneath that where I've mentioned RR. RR is the respiratory rate, which was measured at between 70 and 90 breaths per minute. It was also noted that she had what we call subcostal recessions. Subcostal recessions are when the skin underneath the lungs is being pulled backwards and forwards because she is breathing quite hard.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So that is a visual sign or a visual indicator of --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Respiratory distress, that she was needing extra support.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Going back to the data, the respiratory rate of 70 to 90, is that sub-optimal?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's sub-optimal, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Too quick?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Too high, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. The next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I've said her oxygen saturation levels are between 97% and 99%. They are acceptable.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Scroll down please. This goes on to another page but is this a continuation of your note from the same examination of the baby and her data?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct. It's a discussion with dad, but yes, it's about discussing [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So you informed her father that although her blood tests have improved slightly, as you've just explained to us, you're having to give her a high level of respiratory support in order to maintain her oxygen saturation levels?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: That's a written version of the evidence you gave a few minutes ago effectively; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. You explained to her father that the safest option -- well, you decode all of that for me, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have subsequently had a discussion with [Baby D]'s father and I've explained at this moment in time, given the high level of breathing support that we're having to give in order to maintain her oxygen saturation levels within normal parameters, the most safest thing to do for [Baby D] would be to what we call intubate her, so place her a breathing tube into her airway, and then put her on a ventilator with the hope of actually giving her some medicine and then taking her off of the ventilator relatively quickly.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you help us with the abbreviation WOB?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: WOB means work of breathing.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. So you confirmed in the note that her father understood and confirmed the decision to intubate [Baby D] and then we keep reading. Mr Murphy, if you could help us, please. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So now this is a note of the attempted intubation, is it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Could you --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So it looks like we tried to pass a size 3 endotracheal tube, but we were unable to pass that because [Baby D] was quite active at that time. We then moved to giving her some elective intubation drugs. So these are drugs to settle her, to allow us
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: to pass that -- perform that procedure successfully. So the drugs that we gave would have been as per the clinical guidelines for the drugs we used at the Countess of Chester Hospital at that time, which would have been morphine, atropine and suxamethonium.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Then it looks like Dr Thomas, who was the SHO, the ST1, had an attempt at intubation. She was unable to insert the endotracheal tube because she was unable to get a good visualisation of the cords. And I then subsequently took over and inserted the endotracheal tube at first attempt.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's just go back up a bit, please, Mr Murphy, and we'll go over that ground one more time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You attempted to insert a size 3 tube?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The baby was too active?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So you gave her drugs to make her less active --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- to enable the procedure? And your junior colleague tried and failed to insert the tube but then you successfully inserted it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: What would have been in effect the third attempt?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Then we have some information about the intubation. So it was inserted at 10 centimetres to the lips?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. And then it was subsequently pulled back because we would listen in, we would what we call auscultate or listen in to make sure that the air entry on both sides of the chest was good, so I've asked for it to be pulled back by a centimetre, and I've confirmed that the air entry is good. And the capnograph, which is what is called a colourimetric carbon dioxide detector, it will change from purple to yellow if inspired carbon dioxide is given out, and that's important because it means that the endotracheal tube is in the right place. And that's confirmed.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So she was exhaling carbon dioxide, which demonstrates it's working?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Then secured at that position?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Was it -- what method would you have used to secure it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't remember. It would have been as per the trust's guidelines at that time.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The next entry, "good" -- is that --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Good A/E" means air entry, bilaterally, which means that we are getting air, or oxygen in this case initially, into both lungs when the tube has been secured at 9 centimetres.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. So the intubation process has been completed and is working successfully?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So this is the initial rates that we set the ventilator at. So CMV is the mode of ventilation, continuous mandatory ventilation is what CMV stands for, so that's the ventilator doing the work initially for the baby.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The 22 is what we call the PIP, the peak inspiratory pressure, and that's the highest amount of pressure that we will give on the ventilator. And the PEEP, similar to the reference previously, is the end expiratory pressure and that's the amount of pressure that's being given at the lowest point of the breath.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And the R, that stands for the rate that the ventilator is going to give these breaths at, and that's at 60 breaths per minute. And you can see "in 30% O2", so we were in 30% oxygen at that point.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. So you have recorded in this note how you decided to place [Baby D] on a ventilator?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Although your plan, it seems, was to do so for a relatively short time; was that your intention?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That was the intention but it would be dependent very much on [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And so the equipment was put in place and she was attached to a ventilator and provided assistance at those rates?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Could we please go to tile 35. We understand, Dr Brunton, that part of the protocol in these circumstances would be to obtain a chest X-ray for what purpose?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, in this situation it would be to ensure that the endotracheal tube is in the correct position.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. So if we scroll down, please, we've already looked at this part of the note. Pausing there, we've finished with the page above now, so this is the statement of intention, "To obtain a chest X-ray"; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: You take us from CXR, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: CXR is chest X-ray. If the ET, endotracheal tube, is in a good position, then we would proceed to giving a medicine called surfactant. The next part of the plan was to hold off morphine at present. I didn't want to give morphine at that point because the hope would be that we would be able to take her off the ventilator pretty quickly. Morphine is what we call a respiratory depressant, it would reduce the amount of breaths that a baby would take, so we wouldn't give that unless we were going to be on the ventilator for a longer period of time.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: We then planned to do a repeat blood gas in an hour to see if there was an improvement. As you can see, after that my plan was to speak to the parents regarding that.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The purpose of surfactant?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Surfactant is a protein that is involved in the aid of gas exchange within the lung. What we sometimes find with babies, particularly babies born prematurely, but it can happen with babies who are born at term as well, they can be deficient of surfactant. There's no way of actually knowing this without looking at the clinical parameters of the baby and my concern at that time was that with a high oxygen concentration and still needing quite a bit of non-invasive respiratory support, potentially [Baby D] would benefit from getting some surfactant,
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: so we gave that medicine down the endotracheal tube subsequently.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The resultant image was reviewed by you --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- at -- now we're at 23.00 hours, 11 pm, still on the Saturday night. Your finding was?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My finding was -- as you can see it says:
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: "ET tube position..."
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Again referring to the endotracheal tube position and it was slightly high, so I pushed it in -- when I say high it was sitting within the airway but not at the level that we would like, so I pushed it in by approximately 0.75 centimetres. And then I've made some general comments around the X-ray itself, which showed no obvious signs of consolidation, so any obvious signs of infection within the chest X-ray. There was no obvious signs of a pneumothorax, which is an air leak from the lung cavity -- within the lung cavity, sorry.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And I have said that it is, "Likely RDS", which is what I referenced earlier, which is a condition called respiratory distress syndrome, "type picture".
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So you undertook the bedside review of the X-ray image?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Was it protocol that, subsequently, a radiologist colleague would make a further examination of the same image and provide feedback to you, the clinicians?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, they would do that. I think -- again, I can't remember the exact parameters of how -- the mechanism of how it worked, sorry, in the Countess of Chester. But again this was taken out of hours on a Saturday night, so this would be subsequently reported in the following few days.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: At the same time as you have timed your review of the Xray, that is to say 23.00 hours, we see alongside your name and I think in your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Tell us about this?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So Curosurf is the brand name for surfactant and that is the medicine, the protein. It's given in a liquid form and it was given down the endotracheal, down into the lungs to actively take an effect on the lungs. The batch number is just the number of the medicine that we give. We like to record it.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: An audit trail. Then 15 minutes later?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So it looks like then I've spoken to [Baby D]'s mother and father. I've explained that [Baby D] is clinically stable at present, although is on a ventilator, and I have explained that I'm awaiting a repeat blood gas to review to see if we can reduce the level of support on the ventilator at that time that we are, I am presuming that is going to say, currently giving.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: I think we need to go to the next tile, please, to see the continuation of that note. So behind -- thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There is a continuation of the same note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then I've explained that -- the fact that if there is prolonged ventilation required, or a deterioration or [Baby D] is not getting better, then we may have to think about transferring her at that point to either Arrowe Park Hospital, which is what APH stands for, or LWH is Liverpool Women's Hospital, and the parents understood that and had no further questions at that time.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Can we break that into two parts. Why would prolonged ventilation, if it were required, cause a transfer?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, it doesn't necessarily definitely happen, that's why I said it may need to happen. But what we think about in these situations is: is this the most appropriate place for a baby who's requiring this level of support to be looked after? We know that Chester was at that time was what we call a level 2 neonatal unit, or a local neonatal unit. They would look after babies -- I can't remember the exact parameters now, but I think it was around 28 weeks' gestation and above or babies who were reasonably stable. If it was demonstrated that [Baby D] was more unwell and requiring more levels of support from an intensive care perspective she would need to be transferred to a higher -another hospital that can provide a higher level of neonatal intensive care.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's continue down the page. Again your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Timed now at 01.50 so we're into the early hours of Sunday, 21 June. It would appear that further blood gas data had been received; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Could you walk us through it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What we can see here is the repeat blood gas again -although I have not got any arrows this time -- has shown a clinical improvement. Her pH has increased to 7.32, which is closer to normal range. And the inspired carbon dioxide level is now 5.44, which is decreased, and that would be close to again normal range. The base excess is within acceptable parameters of minus 4 to minus 5. Her glucose level, which is obviously a measure of her blood sugar, is 6.1, which is again normal. Her lactate was 2.6, which was stable.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So comparing these blood gas readings to the last, do any of them indicate a deterioration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Do all of them indicate an improvement?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The base excess, again, is within acceptable limits but all of the other ones indicate an improvement to me.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's look to the right of this endorsement.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Explain that to us.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So what I've mentioned here is that we've switched the mode of ventilation -- so again I mentioned previously continuous mandatory ventilation. What I've switched to now is synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation, and this is essentially to allow [Baby D] to start to breathe by herself on the ventilator. So the ventilator will support her but she can take some breaths as well.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Can you recall why you made that decision at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Because we had seen a clinical improvement and also I was able to wean her ventilation. As you can see later on in the second sentence, and I will explain that if required, that the hope then would be that allowing her to do that would put her in a position to potentially be able to come off of the ventilator in reasonably short fashion.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Your next entry to the right of the page?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That confirms what I said, that she was putting in multiple breaths by herself.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The next entry is a summary, is it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. It essentially says she remains clinically stable on the ventilator and we were actually reducing the level of respiratory support at that time, so we had weaned the pressures -- the initial starting pressure that we had had been weaned down to a top pressure now of 16, so we were giving her less ventilation to keep her numbers within the optimal ranges. What we did notice however was that on the gas machine we can get a bilirubin level and the bilirubin level at that time was high at 92 and that required treatment and she was currently on the treatment there, as you can see, of triple phototherapy. That's how we treat jaundice levels.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Unfortunately, two of the lab samples that had been sent earlier in the evening had haemolysed, that would be not an unusual thing to happen --
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: What does that mean?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, I don't.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Right. Sorry to interrupt you again, Mr Driver.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Not at all, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Go back to the carousel, please, Mr Murphy, and let us please go to tile 222. You'll see, Dr Brunton, it's timed at approximately 02.35 that morning, where we see firstly what appears to be a review undertaken by you of an X-ray.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So I've documented the review, but what I've written in the notes is "Reviewed by Dr Newby, consultant".
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So this was -- and we can see this is at 02.35, so Dr Newby's note of her attendance at [Baby D]'s bedside was at 2 am?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And at 2.35, you've noted the fact that Dr Newby reviewed an X-ray?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And then is this your writing beneath?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I've written that the UVC, the umbilical venous line, which was used to give the administration of fluids and medicines, was what we call low lying, so it was in a lower position than where had sat previously on X-ray. And I've then commented underneath that there was nothing else of note on the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. The entries below the pro forma X-ray review, are they your entries?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I would have been coming back to review her regularly because she had been unwell previously.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Take us through the set of data.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: These bloods show that the clotting factors were slightly suboptimal. Her prothrombin time was increased slightly and her APTT, which is activated partial thrombin time, was also increased slightly as well. We would have to take that result in clinical context, so you'd be looking, for example, to see -clotting factors are important in whether or not a baby was having issues with bleeding, for example, so you would then have to look at the clinical context of that result to determine whether or not you would need to start any treatment.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And what was the clinical context for this baby at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was the baby having any episodes of obvious overt bleeding? And the answer to that was no. It's not unusual that babies can have slightly abnormal clotting factors in the first 24 to 48 hours and they gradually improve as time progresses. We give babies vitamin K because we know that they can be deficient of vitamin K, for example, at birth.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Can you continue to take us through these entries in your clinical notes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Her sodium level was 129, so that had improved compared to the previous result that we had seen before.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Her potassium level, we now have a result for that, and that was 4.1. Her bicarbonate level was 14, again within parameters that wouldn't require any treatment at the moment. And her urea level was 5.1, and her creatine level was 79, which had improved slightly as well.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: I've not documented all of the LFTs in the top right corner just there. Her liver function tests were -- N means normal when I am documenting things. Her lactate, as you've already discussed, was slightly elevated at 2.75, and her CRP was 6.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Meaning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Meaning that the level 6 -- there's no really any other way of describing it. It's not a high level. We would normally — as per current guidance, and I think guidance at the time, as well, CRPs of 10 and above would be something that we would be...
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Remind the jury what a CRP reading is, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: CRP is C-reactive protein. It's a type of protein that can be a non-specific potential sign of infection.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then what I've documented after that is a repeat gas and I've written post bolus, so after the fluid bolus that I'd asked for previously had been given, and that showed again that the pH was now continuing -- I can't remember the exact number previously but was within acceptable parameters of 7.31. The CO2, the carbon dioxide level, was 5.01, I think, which is again within acceptable parameters. And the base excess is slightly on the elevated side at minus 6.9 to minus 7, which is why I have circled it. The glucose level is within normal parameters at 6.6, and you can see that we have now got a lactate reading from the gas machine and that level is actually lower than the serum sample that was taken at 2.3.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Having considered all of that data, did you then express an assessment as to her evolving condition in the next line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I came back -- and I don't know if I carried out a clinical examination but she had much improved from a clinical perspective. The areas of discolouration, as I've documented there, had completely disappeared.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: I don't know what I've said after that, but it says, "Note above gas".
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: You told us earlier as to the areas of discolouration that it was something that you hadn't encountered, hence you brought in Dr Newby.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct. And I have subsequently, what I've done here is underneath I've said, "Discussed with Dr Newby". I don't know whether I've discussed that with her on the telephone at home or whether I've discussed that in the hospital, but she's then given me a plan as outlined.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So that's your joint plan, as it were?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And the plan was?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As I've discussed, not for correction of the coagulation, the results, the PT and the APTT. We'd to leave the UVC in its current position and continue to use it. And the plan had been as previously and that we would subsequently update the parents thereafter.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. The next entry we're going to is at 03.15, but before we look at the detail of your entry, do you recall this part of the events of the morning of Monday the 22nd?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I do remember this a little bit more, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: All right. Let's go away from the notes for a moment then. Do you recall what caused you to attend upon [Baby D] at about 3.15 that morning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I remember being called -- I was on the paediatric ward and I remember being called at this time to say that [Baby D] had had a period where she was upset and crying and that the rash had reappeared and that her oxygen requirement had gone up again briefly at this time.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Pause there if you would. So that was information received by you through the phone?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: From?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm presuming a nurse, but I can't remember who telephoned me.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: In consequence what did you decide to do?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I made my way to go and see [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Again, before we go to the notes, do you recall what you found upon arrival at her cot?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't remember the specifics, but I do remember her being quite agitated and upset, which had been unusual for her because, again, I don't remember her being like that, it was not something that sticks in my mind that she was like that previously when I had examined her before.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Yes? Anything else?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That she had a bit of a rash, but again I can't remember the rash previously, but she had a little bit of a rash present on her trunk, on her abdomen.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: In relation to her rash, we know your original observations as recorded. Subsequently you noted that it had gone?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And now you recall that it had returned?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Are you able to make any comparison between the two times when you observed a rash?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not from my recollection. It would just be from the medical notes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Anything else from memory before we go to the notes about anything to do with [Baby D] at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Just the agitation, the upset from her, which I felt at that time was due to the mask, the CPAP mask that she was wearing.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So let's look at your notes as of 03.15:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Called urgently."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As you indicated.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I've said "to paediatric ward", but just to clarify, I think I meant to the neonatal unit, I was in the paediatric ward.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: From?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: More appropriate.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Does this paragraph detail information observed by you or facts shared with you?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's what I remember being told on the telephone.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: I can't remember if I physically saw those numbers. By the time I've gone to examine her, however, given the length of distance between the units, which was minimal, she's already back in air.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Right. Can you expand upon that for the jury?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: What I've documented?
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Yes, and your last evidence.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So yes, so what's happened is that I've been called and been told that [Baby D] was crying and she had desaturated to a low level, so her saturation levels were 80% and she was requiring 100% oxygen at that time. I've then made my way to the
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- from the paediatric ward to the neonatal unit and what I have observed was that she had a bit of skin discolouration at that time, but I've documented -- I can't remember what it was like previously to compare it with, but I've written that it was not as obvious as previously seen. But I have then subsequently gone on to examine her -- all of this would have been in a relatively short time frame, I don't know the exact minute-to-minute timeline of events, but she appeared distressed on the CPAP. However, she actually appeared clinically well and all of her examination, apart from the skin discolouration of her abdomen, was normal and she had returned completely back to air.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: I know I'm asking you to approximate, but about how long would have passed from you receiving the call to attend upon her and you making these observations and recording these notes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Two to 3 minutes. I don't think it could be any more than that. I don't know in terms of writing the physical notes themselves, but going from the paediatric ward to the neonatal unit was a very short distance.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. You have added two diagrams here. One of the lungs to the left?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: In between the diagrams, there's notes as to the heart readings?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes. So her lungs, again, examined normally, there was no evidence of any added sounds or any issues. Her heart sounds were again normal and on this situation I've only documented the skin discolouration on the abdomen, but I've noted that there was some skin discolouration present and I've documented it as "slight".
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The information illustrated in that diagram, "Skin discolouration, slight", that diagram, is that from your observations or from facts imparted to you by others?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That would have been from my observations because I was there at this point.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Right. Again, this is an invitation to state the obvious, what do the crosses --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The crosses mean the areas where I noted the skin discolouration, which is what the arrow, sorry, should be pointing to.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So that is to the right of the umbilicus?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At the right of the umbilicus, there seems to be a small amount of area in the left upper quadrant and one little cross just heading towards the left lower quadrant.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The uppermost to the right, where would that correspond to on the baby's trunk?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Probably not far from the belly button, just around that area, but I can't be certain of that.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: That's where the arrow is now; yes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, the arrow's down at the right flank, so down kind of close to your kidneys or your pelvis, for example.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And if we take the cursor to the highest cross.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The belly button would be at the middle of the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So that's where that cross -- the highest cross there would be the left upper side, kind of where your gallbladder -- not your gallbladder, your spleen would be.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Perhaps not all of us know precisely where the spleen might be. Around the ribcage?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Around the ribcage, slightly below.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: I think the belly button --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: The belly button is in the middle.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- (overspeaking) that's the bit where the belly button would be and then you can work out the rest.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, that would be correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So having been called urgently, what was her clinical presentation? Was this an emergency situation on your assessment or not?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, by the time I arrived, there was a clear clinical change in her from being called to when I'd arrived in terms of there being a slight improvement with her. And my particular worry and concern, as you can see there, was that although she still had this rash she was actually quite distressed on the CPAP and there was not any clinical evidence to my mind at that time to keep her on the CPAP. So the plan had been to trial her off of CPAP at that time, as you can see, to see if that would help her in terms of allowing her to be less agitated.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And you drafted a plan?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, which was -- sorry.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Yes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Which was to take her off of the CPAP and also, because the skin discolouration had reappeared, was to try her with a little bit of extra fluid, so give her another bit of fluid to try and increase the perfusion of her skin, and then again to repeat a gas in 1 hour to see if that had improved the situation.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: In your mind or on your professional assessment, what was the potential link between fluids and the skin discolouration?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: My worry was that she -- as we talked about previously, that she maybe didn't have enough fluids on board, so to speak, to provide enough circulation to the organs and the skin, so what I decided to do was to give her a little bit of extra fluid to try and top that up, to see if there would be a benefit or an improvement.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Had you previously encountered babies with a fluid deficiency?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Had you previously encountered skin discolouration of this ilk?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Scroll down to make sure there's no further entries.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. Back to the carousel, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'll just go along in time, pausing briefly at tile 238. We don't need to go behind it. This is just a swipe data entry, Dr Brunton, to inform us of your movement or at least the movement of your pass.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could click behind it briefly. At 03.22, you are, it would seem, or the evidence suggests, you're entering the maternity ward. Then back to the carousel, please. We'll see other similar entries at 245. And then 246. We'll look to see where you are at this point in time. Again, it was suggested that you were passing into the maternity ward through the doors there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Now, please, Mr Murphy, could you take us to tile 253. Sorry, just go back to the carousel for a moment, please. We can see that you've made some notes for events at 03.55, albeit the notes were made retrospectively at 04.35. And we can see, if we look to the right on the next tile, that there's some bleep data to indicate a call was put out for you, to which you responded, we can see, if we went behind the next tile, to see you entering the neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Let's go behind tile 253, please. Thank you. And look at our exhibit J2226. Before we look at the detail, Dr Brunton, do you recall these events?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I recall aspects of them, I don't recall all of them.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Do you recall being summoned to [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Do you recall what was said to you at that point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I recall just being asked to come urgently to see [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: I can't remember the exact wording.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Do you remember what you saw upon arrival?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: When I read -- and as I was walking there, the crash page, I remember going off in the corridor between the paediatric ward and the neonatal unit, so I ran as I was already on the way. And when I arrived, I remember there being Caroline Oakley, who was the nurse looking after [Baby D] that night, I think, and then Emily Thomas, who was the senior house officer, the junior doctor, were around [Baby D]'s bed space (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. Pause there. Does it follow from what you've just told us that you received two signals, as it were?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, definitely, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The first through?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The first through just a normal -- I presume it was a normal page and then I answered the telephone -- I did a telephone call based on that page and then the second one, as I was leaving to go and see her, was a crash page, so an urgent, urgent attendance, so to speak.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: As you recall, Nurse Caroline Oakley and Dr Emily Thomas were present at the cot side. From recollection what were they doing?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't quite remember exactly who was doing what but I remember them both being around the cot space because [Baby D] was unwell at this time.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And in general terms, what sort of treatment were they providing to the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: They were providing emergency treatment.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And did you join in?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Before we look at the notes, are you able to give us an account, a summary, of what happened?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, at that time when I arrived, she -- I don't believe she had a heart rate or -- I can't -- to be honest I can't remember, without reviewing my medical notes, exactly the timeline.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Let's review your medical notes. The timing of 04.35 is the timing of the making of the note --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, written in retrospect.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- for events that your first entry informs us took place at or around 03.55?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: So you were called to the neonatal ward and you have noted -- please take us through after the time 03.55?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was called to the neonatal ward. I had been told that [Baby D] had an apnoea, which is a pause in her breathing, and was struggling to saturate, so get her oxygen saturations levels within appropriate levels. As I've documented, I left the children's ward immediately and as I was attending the neonatal unit, the crash page went off. I've subsequently walked on to the unit and chest compressions, I don't know who by, were being commenced, and at that time on the monitor [Baby D]'s oxygen saturation levels were between 60% and 70% and she had a heart rate of between 60 and 70.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Pausing there, forgive me once again for inviting you to state the obvious, but what do those readings mean?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: They mean that she's not very well.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As you can see, I have immediately taken over the airway, because when we're resuscitating babies, children, adults, the airway is the most important thing to try and improve situations like this. And I carried out a clinical assessment.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And were you the most senior clinician at the cot side at that point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At that point in time, yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And does protocol dictate that you take the lead?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And you did so?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: At that time I have assessed the heart rate was less than 60, there was no chest wall movement, so [Baby D] wasn't obviously breathing, and she had a lot of secretions. I can't remember whether those secretions were from the mouth or from the nose, but at that time I knew that she was very unwell, so I've asked for the nursing staff to call Dr Newby, who was the on-call consultant.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Thank you. We'll then go through the timeline minute by minute as recorded, but if I may digress for a moment.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recall that there was something of an error or some confusion in terms of the communication through the telephone?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. As per my police statement, I was standing at [Baby D]'s airway trying to manage that, when a phone was placed to my ear. I might need my statement just...
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Do your best for the moment. We'll help you if need be.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: But the phone was placed to my ear and within a few seconds I realised that the person that I was speaking to was not Dr Newby on the phone.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Right. So that conversation was stopped?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, within seconds.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And you returned to providing emergency treatment to the baby.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. The emergency treatment was ongoing, it never stopped.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Of course, my mistake. Is the process that one of the team record the events contemporaneously, minute by minute, event by event?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That would be normally what would happen, a scribe in effect.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And that enables you or assists you to provide this detailed record after the events looking backwards?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: And we can see what happened in the minutes that followed. So at 03.58?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I passed a breathing tube again down into [Baby D]'s airway, we got a capnograph positive, which again means that the breathing tube was in the correct place, and we got good chest wall movement, so the chest was starting to rise. Our chest compressions were continuing at this time.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Pause there, Dr Brunton. The good chest movements, was that indicative of the baby breathing for herself --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- or a consequence of your intervention?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's a consequence of my intervention.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: At 04.00 hours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We gave a dose of adrenaline and that was given via the umbilical venous catheter.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: That was intended to do what or --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Try and stimulate the heart rate.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: We gave a second dose of adrenaline, again via the umbilical venous catheter.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: We gave some fluid to try and increase the circulatory volume. That was 10ml per kilo of 0.9% sodium chloride, so a standard fluid bolus, and that was given via the umbilical venous catheter.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Another dose of adrenaline was given at the same dose as previously via the umbilical venous catheter.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, I think to see the continuation of this note we need to go behind tile 264. It's just the way it's been set out. If we go over to the next page, so we've just gone from time 04.05 to time 04.07.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have documented at this time that Dr Newby is now in attendance, a fourth dose of adrenaline is given via her umbilical venous catheter, and we gave a first dose of sodium bicarbonate via her umbilical venous catheter to try and correct any acidity levels that will have now built up in the blood.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: That was what it was hoped the sodium bicarbonate might address --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: -- if needed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: We gave a fifth dose of adrenaline via the umbilical venous catheter.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: We gave another dose of sodium bicarbonate via the umbilical venous catheter.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: We gave another fluid bolus again to try and increase the circulating volume of fluid round [Baby D]'s body.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: That was a standard dose given via umbilical venous catheter.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: Dr Newby then asked to increase the adrenaline dose, which we can do from 0.1 to 0.3 mics per kilo, done via the UVC, and another bolus of fluid was given via the umbilical venous catheter.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON

blocks.text: The fact that you were returning -- repeating, forgive me, adrenaline dose after adrenaline dose and now at this stage the quantity of the dose was increased, why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Why was all that necessary?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: All of that was necessary because [Baby D] was in effect dying in front of us.
blocks.speaker: BRUNTON
