blocks.text: Caring for women during pregnancy, essentially, particularly with high-risk conditions, so problems with previous pregnancies and then women who have pre-existing
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: medical disorders. And then sort of -- the sort of clinical, administrative and management role within that which then also involves reviewing case incidents.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Your focus is on the mother?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Is that both pre and post-natally?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Do you have any responsibility for the child once the child is delivered?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: With that in mind, you've been asked to provide a statement concerning the treatment of [Mother of Baby D] during the birth of her daughter [Baby D] back in June 2015. I don't think you actually met [Mother of Baby D] until, sadly, after [Baby D]'s death at the hospital.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: But you have used notes to put together a history of the treatment that she received; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Thank you. And we will go to those notes in a moment, but was [Mother of Baby D]'s pregnancy considered a low or a high-risk pregnancy?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was a low-risk pregnancy.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Are you aware she attended on routine occasions?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think there was a couple of attendances for fairly routine stuff.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: We've heard that she presented for the first time to the hospital at 36 weeks and 6 days' gestation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And her presentation was with ruptured membranes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: We just heard that at the time she attended the hospital in that regard, she was very close to 37 weeks' gestation.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think short of about 12 hours.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Is that a significant milestone?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Why's that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Essentially, term is 37 weeks and above, and preterm is below 37 weeks.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Okay. You have confirmed that [Mother of Baby D] was admitted to the labour ward for induction at just after midnight on 16 June 2015; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think when I looked at that statement I think that date is wrong. I think it was 20 June she actually got admitted to the --
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Thank you. And the indication at that stage was a spontaneous rupture of the membranes the previous day?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: If we could go to those notes, please. They're going to appear on a screen before you. They're the basis for your statement and I'll take you through them.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, these notes don't have the J numbers that everyone's become familiar with yet. They are paginated so we'll rely on the pages as they appear for now, but we'll ensure it's replaced with the appropriate document.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Hopefully, we can see at the bottom that the first of these pages is numbered 240. Could you describe what these notes are, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: These are handwritten maternity notes and they -- it obviously has [Mother of Baby D]'s name at the top and these are notes taken -- it looks like a midwifery signature.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: The top part of it is -- we use standardised stickers to relay certain documentation and then the second part of the note is midwifery notes with regards to labour. And then the first doctor entry is the sort of different handwriting occurring (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: If I can just ask you to pause there.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Could you sit closer to the microphone and keep your voice up? In fact, would you mind pulling the microphone slightly towards you? The request is because someone is transcribing what you're saying in a different room and they're having difficulty hearing.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm going to take you to the notes you relied upon in compiling your statement and I am going to ask you to just explain in brief terms what each of the notes means and that will present hopefully the chronology that you've relied on in your document.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If we can turn, please, first to, on this document, page number 240, which I think we're at, and if we go to the lower part, there's an entry at 02.50 hours. Could you explain that note to us, please?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. As you can see, it's dated and timed, as you would expect, and it's an entry made by ST1, which is the level of doctor, which is the first year of a junior doctor who is specialising in obstetrics and gynaecology. I think the name is Bhatt. It's her entry of her review at that time. So P0 means it's a lady on her first pregnancy. She has put she's 37 plus 1 at that point. "SROM" refers to spontaneous rupture of the membranes on 18 June at 04.00. They are clear and a little bit pink and she's referred to two times Prostin with a tick to means that she has had two Prostins.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Pause there for a moment: spontaneous rupture of membrane, just explain that to us, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Part of the labour process is that the waters go, that's the more generic term. Sometimes the waters go before labour starts, as in this case, and labour then doesn't follow. Or sometimes they go actually in the middle of labour.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Right. So I think you described it as waters breaking.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's perhaps what more of us may recognise it as. The significance, please, of the note that, presumably this is the fluid, is clear and pink?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You use that as a marker of whether there's any concern about the baby. So you might be concerned if there was what's called meconium, which is baby's poo, which could suggest the
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: baby had been in distress. You also might be looking for very heavily bloodstained liquor which might mean there had been bleed behind the placenta, or you might be looking for offensive liquor that perhaps looks like pus, which you might see with an infection.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So that's why the doctor's written that it was clear, pinky. Clear is completely normal, pinky is the sort of the -- it's very slightly blood tinged, usually from the cervix starting to dilate. That's when we get that appearance.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Two times Prostin?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the treatment for -- because she hadn't gone into labour, then we then want to bring the labour on, or induce the labour, and the management of that is a prostaglandin, which is the hormone treatment which is goes into the vagina to start the process of labour.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And the treatment at that time was for two separate doses of the prostaglandin into the vagina. So that refers to -- that's been given.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: That indicates that treatment started with two administrations?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. She would have had one and then, 6 hours later, she would have had a second one so that process generally takes at least 12 hours.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Okay. These notes don't flow altogether chronologically. So if we could go next to page 255.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The next entry you rely on is given by Dr Bhatt on the same shift, 20 June, at 07.15. You have commented on the CTG assessment being reassuring. Can you explain that for us please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So CTG stands for cardiotocograph and it is a foetal heart monitor that sits on to the lady's abdomen, monitoring the foetal heart and also monitoring if there any contractions. And what this sticker is here -- as a doctor you go and look at the tracing that is produced and you look at various factors within it, which you can see she's circled. And then she's come to the conclusion from that circling that the factors altogether was that the CTG at that time was reassuring.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Temperature's recorded?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. You can see that there's other factors on this sticker. The maternal pulse is within the normal range of. The temperature is normal at 36.6. At this time her contractions are
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: recorded at about one every 10 minutes. Still reports that the liquor or the fluid is clear and the reporting at that time is that she's 2 centimetres dilated.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: If we scroll down that page, any other information on that particular page?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So essentially when you go as a doctor to review a patient the whole thing is to look at the whole picture, so it's quite common to rewrite again what you know about the case so far. So Dr Bhatt has written "progress" and she's reiterated the SRM or the rupture of membranes or the waters have gone at 04.00 on 18 June. She's put that she was 2 centimetres at 03.00 on 20 June and in brackets that was after the two lots of the prostaglandin or Prostin. She's had then Syntocinon, which is an intravenous infusion to bring on the labour and she's said that started at 03.05. And now she's reporting that she's still 2 centimetres dilated at 07.05 and she's put there that the dose of the oxytocin at this time was 60ml per hour.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And dilation, please, the significance of it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There's no change from the previous examination.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Okay. What does the dilation in short refer to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: You need to be 10 centimetres dilated to have a baby.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So you go from a completely closed cervix to slowly progressing to 10 centimetres.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Right, okay. In light of everything that Dr Bhatt has noted is there a plan set out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. She's planned at this point to increase the dose of oxytocin up to the maximum rate, which is 96ml per hour, planned to re-examine in 4 hours, and to aim for contractions to be four to five every 10 minutes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: The next note on which you comment appears at page 257, please. It's timed at 08.50. Dr Dinardo's note we can see in the slightly bolder manuscript.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, this was at 08.50 and it's a routine consultant ward round by Dr Dinardo, which is routinely done on everyone on the labour ward.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Pausing there, Dr Dinardo's position, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She's also a consultant obstetrician and gynaecologist in the unit.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Thank you. Sorry to interrupt.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So again you can see she's taken a brief summary of the case. So a 32-year-old lady -- primate means first pregnancy -gestation 37 plus 1., BMI is weight of 29.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Again, she's put then when the ruptured membranes occurred on 18 June that the induction of labour process -- that's -- the IOL stands for "induction of labour" -- started on 19 June, with the two times Prostin. BS stands for Bishop score. This is a score that we use of the cervix when we are doing induction of labour because dilation isn't the only important thing, there are other factors such as how soft the cervix is and the position of the cervix. So she was merely defining what the score of the cervix was.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: What does 3 tell you about that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Quite unfavourable still at that point. So certainly not in active labour at that point.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Then she's said, however following that score, we then started the Syntocinon drip, which was commenced at 03.00, and that she had been on the 96ml, which is the maximum rate, since 08.00. So it had been -- it gets increased every half an hour incrementally and that's what had been happening over the night. She's written that the contractions are irregular, which would suggest to me that we're still not in established labour, that the pains are mild, and she has written the internal os is closed, 2 centimetres long, and the head is minus 3.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: What that is referring to this sort of Bishop score. So the neck of the womb, you've got an outside bit and the inside bit, from that she thinks the inside bit is still actually closed although the outside bit has been slightly opened by the initial drugs. The head refers to how low the head is coming down into the vagina and by minus 3 it's still quite high up in the pelvis.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And she has put "query forewaters", which -- when the waters have gone, sometimes they can go up from high up at the top part of the uterus and you get the fluid coming out, which is why she was being induced. But sometimes the bit in front of the baby's head that you can feel vaginally hasn't got a hole in it and it's like a balloon full of fluids and sometimes you have to then go back and try again to see if you can make another hole in the forewaters, which is the bit just in front of the head.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Pausing there, the membrane is ruptured, some of the fluid is drained, but some may -- this is the query -- have collected near the baby's head and not been able to escape?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Again, from Dr Dinardo there's a plan.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So she said:
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: "Repeat the vaginal examination at 11.00."
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And I think that relates to -- the last examination had been 4 hours before that, so you would normally do an examination every 4 hours.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: The next note upon which you comment appears at page 260, please, and is timed at 11.25. I think this is an entry from a Dr Pelicaric(?); is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, I don't know and I've never met Dr Pelicaric.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: He was doing a locum shift that weekend, I think.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Again what --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Harder to read this one!
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: The elements upon which you've commented upon:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "CTG reactive."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Which I think we can see six lines down.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. He's done the same again, he's done a summary of what's happened so far and at this point he's put:
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: "CTG reactive, normal trace."
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: He's put the PV, which is vaginal examination, he has put:
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: "Cervix 1 centimetre. Long, very posterior.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: 1 centimetre dilated. Head is high and blotting."
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So that refers to what I was talking about before: you can still feel the head high up in the pelvis rather than low in the vagina. He's put "clear" but then in brackets he has put:
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: "Bloodstained liquor draining."
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: It seems to -- what does that tell us? That seems to be almost contradictory.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It does seem to be contradictory, yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: I think the other comment you've made at that stage in respect of this is:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Contacting (sic) well on Syntocinon."
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So higher up he's put, he says:
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: "On Syntocinon from today."
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And then he has put:
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: "Contracting well for the last 2 to 3 hours where it was just tightening before."
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So we have started this drip but we start at a very low dose and we build it up slowly and by looking at the situation it would appear that the contractions had become increasing both in timing and in strength, which is what you'd expect from the drug that we're giving.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So it's only really been for the last 2 to 3 hours that we're starting to have regular, stronger contractions.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Okay. Now, below that sentence that we discussed a moment or two ago, I think it says "both couple tired". Just expand on that for us, please, if you can.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Well, I think -- I can only read what you can:
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: "Both couple are tired and asking for an emergency caesarean section."
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Which I think is understandable. They've obviously been in the hospital for 2 days now and they are no closer to having their baby. That's what we try to do in labour, is have a two-way conversation. So they've obviously verbalised that and the doctor's written a conversation with [Mother of Baby D], the situation explained.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: The situation really being at this time that we're only just starting to get her into labour, we're only just starting to get regular contractions. And then it goes on to say:
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: "We would advise that we plan to continue with vaginal delivery for the next 3 to 4 hours and then make a final plan."
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And then he has written there obviously he's left them to chat face-to-face, ie we, as medical staff, left them alone to discuss that advice that we gave them.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Okay. The next note that you comment upon is presumably the next review because it's at 3.10 that afternoon and it's at page 265. It's the same handwriting, so it's Dr Pelicaric again. Again you've commented that the CTG is reactive.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Is that a normal trace?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: "CTG reactive, normal trace, and contracting well on Syntocinon."
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: However, the vaginal findings are very similar to previously, with only 1 centimetre dilated. So there's a conversation with the couple. Obviously the patient and the husband are very tired and feels that...
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: (Pause). Not sure what that says. But asking for emergency caesarean section, which was decided as the plan to go ahead with and at this point he then called the theatre team, did the consent form, and informed the consultant and then made the decision to do a category 2 emergency caesarean, which was within an hour.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Okay. We know that an emergency caesarean followed that afternoon. And you from the maternity notes, although they're not now available to you, were able to check the initial details of the birth. And that of course is where your responsibility ceased as far as [Baby D] was concerned.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Where there is a poor outcome, for example a death with a child in these circumstances, is it the normal course of events to conduct a review?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And was a review carried out in the case of [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: What's the purpose of the review?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think several purposes. The first purpose is to try and ascertain from a patient safety point of view what has happened and to make sure that there has not been any sort of
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: individual member of staff working outside of guidelines that should not be carrying on with work.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: That's a very rare finding from a review, but that is sort of the priority, initially, from a safety point of view.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And then the second is from a learning point of view -- again, it might be if there was a guideline that was perhaps difficult and it wasn't reading well that the sooner we discovered that, we could put that into place for the next shift, that that would be important to do.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And thirdly, it's -- obviously you've got two parents who are grieving and the sooner you can try and give them some information, if there's any to be had, that also helps the basis of your conversation with them afterwards.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Okay. Bearing in mind you told us about your -- the parameters of your responsibility, did your review concentrate on any particular aspect of the care?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So our review would have been entirely from the minute [Mother of Baby D] became pregnant to the minute she delivered, so it would have been purely obstetric care, whereas my neonatal colleagues concentrated on the care of [Baby D] as soon as she was born. So I was very much up to the point of delivery.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Is that an unusual way to divide the responsibilities or is that --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. We do joint reviews all of the time because that's — we have different areas of expertise and we also then get other people in. So for instance if -- sometimes we get an anaesthetist in if it's relevant, sometimes we get theatre staff in if it's relevant, depending on what the incident is.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Would you ever comment on the neonatal side of things?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I wouldn't, unless -- as I say, we do joint reviews so we're meant to -- we obviously get some expertise of what is normally picked up, so if I saw something glaring that I didn't think somebody else had seen, I'd say, "Have you considered this?" But in this particular case, as far as I remember, I think we did it separately, so I wasn't there for the neonatal review.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And the outcome of your initial review, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The initial review showed that her care antenatally and during labour had followed the guidelines.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: All right. Was that the end of the review? Was there a further review?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we do an immediate incident review -- so this is done -- it's usually supposed to be done within 72 hours of the incident to get that sort of urgent immediate learning. And then you then do a more in-depth review and the case at that particular time used to be discussed -- taken and discussed at a joint meeting between obstetricians, midwives and paediatricians.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Limited to Chester?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry?
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Limited to Chester or on a wider scale?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At the time in 2015 it was limited to Chester.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Okay. And what was the outcome of that further review?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So on presenting the case, as far as I remember I think it was one the senior midwives at the time just said, well, she wasn't 37 weeks therefore she wasn't what we would call a term rupture of membrane, she was a preterm rupture of membranes, therefore the guideline wasn't completely followed. And it was one of those discussions where probably half the people in the room said, well, we don't think that because she was 12 hours off 37 weeks, and the other half of the room said, well, she was in theory a premature rupture of membranes, therefore the guideline wasn't completely followed.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So up to 37 weeks, the guideline says antibiotics?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, sorry, up to 37 weeks, then the additional thing would have been to start oral antibiotics on diagnosis of the waters going.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Right. But here there was some disagreement given the proximity of the rupture to that 37-week point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. Because the commonest people we're seeing with preterm rupture of membranes are anything -- we see people from 30 weeks, you know, 34 weeks, so you know this was very unusual that it was literally the 12 hours before.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And what is the risk when membranes rupture?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The risk is the same whether you're preterm or term of infection. So the membranes are a barrier between the outside
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: world and inside the uterus. So when they go, you get an increased risk of infection.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Okay. Does that risk of infection progress proportionately or consistently or does it accelerate as time goes by?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's meant to be worse after 24 hours. The risk starts to get worse 24 hours after. That's the sort of guideline for a term rupture of membranes. A preterm rupture of membranes, they're sort of -- there's people who have ruptured membranes for many days and many weeks sometimes that we manage and some people never get infected and other people get infected very quickly.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: I think in this case there was a longer than 24-hour period between membrane and birth -- sorry, rupture of membrane. Was that a significant feature to have in mind?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's not. So the guideline is -- is that you leave somebody -- if -- for 24 hours to see if they labour by themselves, because often you get the waters going and then labour happens by itself. So that's why you give the first 24 hours. If at 24 hours the waters -- they haven't gone into labour, that's when you offer to induce somebody, but we have to accept that the induction process takes at least 24 hours in the majority of women, particularly in their first pregnancy. So it is not unusual to find somebody perhaps reaching their third day after the waters have gone before they've had a baby.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: With all those features in mind what conclusion, if any, was reached by that second review?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think the only conclusion was is -- that we missed giving an oral antibiotic the night that [Mother of Baby D] came in.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: That would have been the guideline for preterm rupture of membranes. The next part of the guideline is that you then arrange to induce somebody when they are 37 weeks. So we would not have delivered her any sooner, we would not have induced her any sooner, and the care during labour would not have been any different. So the difficulty that we have at the meeting was saying, well, we didn't feel that one dose of oral antibiotic would have changed the outcome because the oral antibiotics are obviously a very low dose antibiotic.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Was there any evidence of infection at [Baby D]'s birth?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No. I mean the whole -- during labour, labour is monitored very carefully so there are observations done throughout labour. And in particular, in this situation, when you've got ruptured membranes you are looking for signs of infection that you can either treat with intravenous antibiotics or, if you're worried about a baby, then in that situation doing a caesarean earlier. That's where I had felt from the initial review that the guideline had been followed, every single observation had been done as it should have been done, and there was absolutely no evidence from [Mother of Baby D]'s temperature, her blood pressure, her -- the liquor we were talking about, there was no evidence of infection from her during the labour. And the CTG, this foetal heart monitoring, that can be the indicator sometimes of infection, for instance some of the parameters change with infection, and that showed absolutely no evidence of infection.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: How would infection have manifested itself at the birth if there had been such an infection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: As I say, I might have expected [Mother of Baby D] herself to show a temperature or a high pulse rate in labour. And then -- certainly when we do the caesarean section, if there's an infection of liquor then you get very offensive smelling liquor when you do the operation or you may even see pus and we saw no evidence of that.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Thank you, doctor. I have no more questions but if you can wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS

Dr Davies, can I just check. You have told us about a review that was conducted into [Mother of Baby D] and [Baby D] after [Baby D]'s death. And you are the -- were you the obstetric and gynaecological lead for that?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I was.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And who was the neonatal lead for that, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm afraid I can't recall.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Was there a neonatal lead for that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As far as I remember.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Would there be a record somewhere of who was the neonatal lead?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Is there any formal record made of the review?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There is, which I refer to in my statement, but I must say I haven't seen it since, many years ago.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Your position was that good care had been provided; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: As I say, it was on that initial review at 72 hours, yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And that trust guidance had been followed?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And that was your view on the initial review?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Did that view ever change?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It did after this joint meeting that we had. I -- I had to agree, yes, she was 12 hours short of 37 weeks.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Did your review come to any conclusions about [Baby D]'s condition at birth?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mine didn't because I don't do a neonatal review.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Right. So although you've been asked questions about evidence of infection at birth for [Baby D] and things like that, your review didn't actually go into looking at the picture for [Baby D] from the point of birth onwards?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: To what extent is the content of this review designed to meet any potential criticism of the hospital arising out of the care of [Mother of Baby D] and, by implication, [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Sorry, I don't understand the question.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Right. Sometimes people may have a complaint about the care they've received; that's true, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: With that in mind, to what extent is the review that you and the neonatal lead are conducting designed to meet any such criticism?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's meant to be a complete and thorough review so that we can then meet with parents and be very clear about what we have found. In 2015 I think those sort of reviews were owned by the trust, whereas nowadays we do do a trust -- a review with an external examiner and there's a much tighter process of sharing that with both the patient and with external...
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Right. Were you, at the time of any aspect of this review, whether it was the earlier one or the later one, were you aware of any criticism or any question of action being taken against the trust by [Mother of Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know to be honest. I met with [Mother of Baby D] and her husband several times and I think we talked about where to go from here, which we always talk about with people about the complaints process and about the legal process and how they can take it further if they wish to. But I don't know if I -- I don't remember being aware if they did take it further that way, especially then when they had their next baby and I was looking after them and I was really totally focusing on that rather than whether they were having a legal action against the trust because I think that obviously mars the case sometimes. So I'm not completely aware if they had a legal action against the trust.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: You were unaware of that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Did you, as part of your part of the review, review the care of [Mother of Baby D] from when she first attended the hospital?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: I'd like to be clear about this: do you accept there were any shortcomings or potential shortcomings in her care?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, she did not get the antibiotics.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Right. There are things I'll ask other witnesses about the condition of [Baby D] after her birth, given what you've said, Dr Davies. I've got them here, I won't ask you because you've explained that at that point you're not involved in that part of the review.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Just on the question of infection then, infection in neonates is a leading cause of death for babies, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And there can be infection arising either because of things that happen during the birth process -- that's one time there can be infection, isn't it? I know you're nodding. You have to say yes or no.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. Infection can arise even before they've started the birth process, so we're finding out more and more now of inflammation that happens long before a lady comes in, a couple of days, you know, in labour, you can then get infection that happens once the waters have gone while you are waiting to labour or during labour.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And then, yes, of course, you can then get infection of a baby once the baby is born.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Yes. Once the baby has left the mother -- and in hospital, infection can be acquired at that time as well, can't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So far as the risk of infection from a mother to a baby is concerned, sometimes, as you've described, you might be able to identify that a mother has an infection, that might be obvious, mightn't it --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: -- from the signs you have talked about? Sometimes if you're looking at things like temperature or heart rate a mother might have an infection and it not be evident from that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right. That's why we would often send the placenta, for instance, which we did in this case, because you might then see the placenta has got huge amounts of pathological changes that you can see under a microscope, which were not present on this placenta.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: But there is always the residual risk of infection passing from the mother, or from some part of her body, within her body, to the child at the time of birth, isn't there?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: There is, yes. That's why the paediatricians do have a set of risk factors that they look for as to which babies they screen for infection.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: If the membranes rupture in a mother, then that is potentially increasing a risk of infection, potentially, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And as you've explained to us, certainly it's recognised that risk of infection increases after 24 hours; that's how you consider it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So it's for that reason that a mother in the position that [Mother of Baby D] was in should be given oral antibiotics; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And whatever the findings, as a matter of fact, the failure to do that does increase the risk of infection, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: For whom?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: For the child.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Um, as I say, I... I... I am in doubt that the 12-hour — 12 hours of one dose of oral erythromycin would have had any effect in this case.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: You may be in doubt, you don't know, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: That's the truth of it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I don't know.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: What we do know, Dr Davies, is that you have guidelines as to when oral antibiotics should be given, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And they're set out in guidance documents for the trust, aren't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They are, yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: They come into two categories. There's a category for the management of rupture of membranes in someone who's preterm and management for the rupture of membranes for someone who is term; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Whether it's by 12 hours or not, as a fact, [Mother of Baby D] came within the preterm rupture guideline, didn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She did.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And it's in that guideline that we see acknowledged the risk of infection from preterm rupture of membranes, don't we?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Just so it's quite clear to the members of the jury, when you've talked about guidance and what have you, the guidance that a mother whose membranes rupture preterm should receive oral antibiotics is set out in that guideline, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It is, yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: You've explained that the risk of infection begins to increase after 24 hours of rupture?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Do you agree that whatever that risk is, by the time there has been a rupture for 60 hours, that is therefore an increase in that level of risk?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And in the case of [Mother of Baby D], by the time of delivery, the membranes had ruptured for 60 hours or had been ruptured for 60 hours, hadn't they?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: They had.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: The remaining questions I have on the topic, my Lord, relate to the question of [Baby D] from the point of birth onwards, so following the evidence of this witness, I won't ask Dr Davies about that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR ASTBURY
Just one question, please, arising. You mentioned the placenta being examined and I think you said there wasn't any. Can I just ask, there wasn't any what?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So the placenta goes for histological examination and essentially, when cells have got infection, then there are numerous changes under the microscope that can be seen. So obviously after [Baby D] died, we spent time waiting to get the
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: results back because we just didn't feel it had acted like infection. Then when we got the post-mortem back and the placental findings back there were just no changes of infection whatsoever in the placenta which you would have been expecting to build up over these 60 hours. So that's plenty of time for the placenta to start showing these changes of infection and it didn't show them.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: You used a phrase "acted like infection". What would you expect if it acted like infection?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm sorry, I don't know...
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: I'll just give you the context of it, thank you. When you got the post-mortem findings and the placental findings you said "it wasn't acting like infection"?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think I meant while we were waiting to find out why she died, I just didn't think infection was going to be the cause because there had been no signs of infection whatsoever. And it was therefore at this joint meeting we had with everyone, it was a surprise to me when they said the pathologist has found congenital pneumonia, and that still didn't make sense to me because there were no other signs of infection throughout anywhere else in [Baby D] and, as I say, in the placenta or the membranes that went to look -- under the microscope.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Further cross-examination by MR MYERS
I wonder if we can clarify one matter arising out of that, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly. There's a matter that I want clarification on. We were talking about infection infection, but it's important to identify the evidence of who had any infection and who didn't have any infection, not who might have got an infection by reason of ruptured membranes and so on. I think it's important to know whether there was any pathological evidence of anyone having an infection.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Let me -- what I wanted to ask is in relation to that so maybe I can deal with it to start with (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'll leave it to you, Mr Myers. If I'm still unclear, I'll ask further questions.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I've asked you about risk of infection. We'll leave risk to one side now and discuss that in terms of evidence found of infection. Taking [Mother of Baby D] first of all, did you
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: identify for sure evidence of infection in her at any stage pre the birth of [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And that relates also to the analysis of the placenta that you undertook?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. The other thing to comment on is that sometimes in these patients -- sorry, the mother's side of things, often you get the temperature and the signs of infection after the baby is born, which we didn't see with [Mother of Baby D]. She didn't develop a temperature at all in those sort of first 24/48 hours after birth either.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Thank you for dealing with that then. The next thing is with [Baby D]. You've made it plain, and I've recognised in the questions that I've asked, that you're not dealing with [Baby D] in the period immediately after her birth and there may be questions to ask there. But you made reference, in answer to questions a moment ago, about congenital pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So can you confirm with us, there was a post-mortem conducted on [Baby D] after her death; that's correct, isn't it? And the finding of the pathologist who undertook that postmortem was that pneumonia was present in [Baby D]; that's correct, isn't it? The pathologist concluded that at that stage cause of death was pneumonia with acute lung injury.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: And it was the opinion of that pathologist, whose name is Dr Jo McPartland, that pneumonia was already present at birth?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: So for those people who aren't familiar with the expressions, you use the expression congenital pneumonia. Congenital means the baby, in this case [Baby D], was born with that condition?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: Which is why on your evidence, Dr Davies, we have the conundrum of you don't identify any specific signs of infection in the mother but you recognise that the post-mortem identified congenital pneumonia in the baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: It's against that background that we've been asking the questions about antibiotics and risk, but my Lord, that's as far as I can take it on the material I have.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Is that clear, my Lord?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, that makes it clearer, the situation.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. That completes your evidence, thank you very much for coming and giving it. You're free to go, but please don't discuss this case with anyone until it's all over —
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: DAVIES

blocks.text: -- and your evidence, obviously.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
My Lord, before a short break, there's a statement to read.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's convenient. Well --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'll read it now and then we don't have to --
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right, read it now. There's another short statement to be read.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Witness statement of ANNA McMANUS (read)
This is a statement from Anna McManus, signed on 25 July 2018:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I am a registered midwife, having qualified in April 2008, and I'm currently employed as a hospital-based midwife at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "On Saturday, 20 June 2015, I worked from 8 am to 8.30 pm. I was involved in the care of [Mother of Baby D], who later gave birth to [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby D]'s waters had broken spontaneously at 36 weeks and 6 days into her pregnancy and it was now 37 weeks and 1 day and she had already started the first part of the induction process.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby D] had been started on a hormone drip to help induce contractions. The frequency of this drip was increased with the intention of making the labour progress and for her cervix to open. [Mother of Baby D]'s observations were monitored and she remained within normal limits throughout her pregnancy. The baby was also continually monitored and hourly assessments were conducted, all of which were normal.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby D] was examined every 4 hours to see how far her cervix had dilated and to see how she was responding to the hormones. It was clear that she hadn't changed much from when she had started the process and following a discussion with the registrar, Dr Conrad, it was agreed that the delivery would be done by caesarean section.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Mother of Baby D] was taken into theatre and during the operation her pain was managed by the anaesthetist, administering medication down the epidural that [Mother of Baby D] already had in place.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The operation was straightforward and uneventful and at 16.01 hours, Baby [Baby D] was born. She was born in good condition and a 2-minute cord clamping delay was utilised to give her extra blood supply and help boost her blood iron levels.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby D] was then shown to her parents before being dried, weighed and generally checked over. There were no concerns for her at this time. The newborn was given an Apgar score at 1 minute of age and 5 minutes of age, each element for heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, response to stimulation and skin colouration can score up to 2 points, giving a maximum of 10 points.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: [Baby D] scored 8 initially due to her colour, she was quite pale and covered in a white vernix. However, after 5 minutes, she started to pink up and I scored her with a 9, with only her extremities remaining pale.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby D] went back to her parents and I checked the placenta to ensure it was complete and that there were no abnormalities to it. When I returned to [Mother of Baby D], I noticed that [Baby D] appeared grey and, on picking her up, she seemed quite floppy. A paediatrician was called and I took her to the Resuscitaire. [Baby D] did not respond to stimulation and I gave her five rescue breaths.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I could see chest movement but she remained floppy.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I then conducted intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) for 2 minutes, after which she started to cry. This can
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: happen to babies that are born by caesarean section as they an still have mucus inside their lungs, which during a normal birth is squeezed out of them and disappears during delivery. This was the thought of Dr Chowdhury, who arrived and examined her shortly afterwards.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was around 5 pm when I noticed that [Baby D]'s grunting that was intermittent and had been quiet was becoming louder and more persistent. [Baby D] was also showing no interest in breastfeeding, and when I gave her a vitamin K injection, she did not react how I would have expected. [Baby D]'s colour had gone off-pink again and although her observations were normal I thought she might have an infection. I decided to contact the registrar, Sarah Rylance, and express my concerns.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was agreed that [Baby D] would be transferred to the neonatal unit for an infection screen. Dr Chowdhury took [Baby D] to nursery number 1 and I followed shortly afterwards to fully brief Dr Rylance. This was the only involvement I had with [Baby D] and I was shocked when a few days later I became aware that she had sadly died."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's the statement of Anna McManus.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We'll have our break now, members of the jury. The next witness is going to be screened, so that will be done during the break, and we'll continue in 10 minutes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (A short break)
I'm sorry that was longer than had been expected. Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: MS LISA WALKER (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR ASTBURY
Can we start with your full name, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's Lisa Anne Walker.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And your profession, please?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Neonatal assistant.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Tell us, please, a little bit about that role.

blocks.text: Okay. So it's a band 4 role. We don't look after intensive care or high dependency, it's just special care babies that we look after.

blocks.text: We've heard a little bit about the structure at the neonatal unit at Chester. Were you employed at Chester, I should confirm, first --

blocks.text: -- back in June 2015. And that there were rooms 1, 2, 3 and 4 --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: -- of varying acuity? Which rooms did you work in?

blocks.text: Three and 4.

blocks.text: What would your roles be in rooms 3 and 4?

blocks.text: Yes, it is.

blocks.text: Would you ever have cause to go into rooms 1 and 2?

blocks.text: All right. How long had you been doing that job at Chester?

blocks.text: I'd been there since 2008.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. And as a neonatal assistant throughout that period?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Now, we've heard a little bit about the shift handover that the nurses would have. Would you be involved in a similar process at the start of each of your shifts?

blocks.text: So like the band 5s and 6s, you would have your own allocated babies, but in rooms 3 and 4 as opposed to the higher acuity rooms?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. Were there certain tasks you could carry out with the babies as opposed to -- or you couldn't carry out with the babies in comparison to the band 5 and 6 nurses?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: We wouldn't look after intensive care babies on CPAP or Optiflow, or obviously intensive care babies on -- intubated or anything like that. It's just special care babies.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And as far as medication, could you administer medication?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The only medication we can administer is vitamins.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. I want to ask you, please, about a baby called [Baby D], okay --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: -- who I think you were able to recall when you provided a statement to the police?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Can you tell us, please, what you recall of baby [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was near to the end of my shift. I was going home and [Baby D] was being brought through from labour ward into neonatal unit.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Let's pause there. She had just come from the labour ward?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: We know that to be 20 June 2015?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: From my statement, yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Yes. Sorry, describe what you saw when you saw [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So I saw the doctor come through -- so there's double doors between the labour ward and neonatal unit. So as I seen him approach the double doors, I opened the door, looked down at [Baby D], and she looked very blue in colour.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Right, okay. And when you saw [Baby D] looking blue in colour, what did you think?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I immediately shouted for help.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. And did help come?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, it did, straightaway.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Do you recall who it was?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I do, yes. It was [Nurse A ].
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: What happened once [Nurse A ] had arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I took the baby off the doctor, wheeled the baby into nursery 1, placed the baby in the incubator on a sats machine and then [Nurse A] asked me to go and get some more help, which -- I went and got help.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. Can you remember which room [Baby D] went in?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She went into room 1.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: What did the doctor do who you'd seen bring her through the double doors?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He looked shocked that I shouted for help and was wondering why I shouted for help.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Do you remember where he went once [Baby D] went into room 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: He followed us into room 1 and sat by the computer.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. What did you make of the doctor's demeanour?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Very -- like he didn't know what was going on, like shocked.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: I think as a consequence of what you saw, you completed a form -- we've heard about Datix forms --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: -- to express your concerns as to what you found?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: All right. Did you have any involvement with [Baby D]'s care once she had been taken into room 1?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: What did you do next?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I just went and got help and then obviously help came and I just left the room then.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: You had your allocated babies in rooms 3 and 4 to continue caring for?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and it was handover time.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Right, okay. You also told the police about another incident that you recalled.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Can you tell us, please, about the other incident that you described?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was working in room 3 at the time, I think there was about three babies and there was myself and Lucy working in there with the allocated babies.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you to pause there because I know the answer to these questions, but do you remember the date this took place?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Do you remember the name of the babies involved?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Are you able to tell us in relation to the incident that you told us about with [Baby D] whether it was before or after?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I... I don't know.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: No, all right. So you can't tell us how long before or after the incident you just told us about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Having interrupted you, I apologise. So you were in the room. Which room was it?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Room 3.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Anyone else in there apart from you and Ms Letby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And how many babies?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think it was three.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Tell us what you recall happening, please.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I was in there at the time, on the left-hand side of the room, and I think Lucy was on the right-hand side of the room. I think we were both feeding babies at the time.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: The saturation monitor alarmed, it goes red and then it alarms, so the baby was desatting.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Let's pause there. So you're feeding a baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: You said Ms Letby is feeding a baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: How was that being done. First of all you, how were you feeding the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: How was Ms Letby feeding the baby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: A nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Right. So just practically, what does that involve for a nurse like you or Ms Letby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: In regards to feeds?
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: To the feeding through a nasogastric tube.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it's obviously a tube that's inserted through your nose, into the tummy, and then babies that can't bottle feed, they get really tired quickly so we use the tube feed. So it's a 10ml syringe that's screwed on to the tube and then the milk is poured in 10ml at a time and it's gravity that takes it.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: We've heard the tube goes through the nose and into the baby's tummy. Where does the syringe attach to the tube?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On the very end.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And is that elevated in some way to make sure that the milk goes in?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. It depends on how you hold it, so with gravity --
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay, it's a syringe. Is it a syringe, would you ever apply pressure to the syringe or does it simply drip through using gravity?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It all depends if there's additives in the feed, if it's Gaviscon or fortifier added then the milk is thickened, so then that would be plunged very slowly, but if it's just milk, it's just gravity.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. So it can be plunged, but only if there's something in the milk, did you say, to make it thicker?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And do you recall on this occasion whether it was simply drip feeding or whether the plunger was being used?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I'm not sure.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: So in relation to where you were, where was Ms Letby?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: On the right-hand side.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Your right-hand side?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Left. I'm left, she's on the right.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: I think in fact you provided the police with a plan of where you were standing when you say this incident happened. If we have a quick look at that, please. If we go to room 3 on the left-hand side of the plan.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you. Do you recognise that handwriting?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: We can see a door on the right of the room. We can see a sink in the far corner.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: I think it's pretty self-explanatory. You've got Ms Letby in the right-hand corner as you would walk into the room; is that right?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And you are in the far left-hand corner from the same doorway?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. There are three marks there. What do those three marks indicate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That's where the cots are with the babies in.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: So that's as you remember the room to be laid out?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: So you're both feeding your respective babies?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And what drew your attention to Ms Letby at that point?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was the alarm going off and the baby desatting and then the baby not picking up, so I went over to help.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: All right. So what would the alarm be attached to?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The baby's foot or hand.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: We've heard about different types of monitors in different rooms.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Are there a particular type of monitor in -- let's take room 3 as the example -- a particular type of monitor there?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: That would be a Masimo, not a Philips monitor. The Philips monitor is like a square TV. This is just a monitor that's on a stand and it only records the heart rate and the saturation levels.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. Is that a fixed monitor or a portable monitor?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's a portable.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Was it the alarm for that device that you were telling us about?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Is there more than one type of alarm or is it just a single tone?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: There's an alarm for a desaturation or an alarm for oversaturation levels. So there's a higher limit and a lower limit.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: That's on the oxygen saturations in the blood as they're being monitored?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: All right. And are you able to say which one it was that went off on that occasion?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It was the lower one, so it was desatting.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. What, if anything, did you do when you heard the alarm activate?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I went over to help.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Is that the thing you would normally do in such a situation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Um, yes, it would, if the nurse -- or if the baby wasn't picking up, yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: So what, if anything, did Ms Letby do when the alarm went off?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She stopped the feed, gave gentle stimulation, and then I think the baby needed some oxygen.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: So we've heard that sometimes a tickle or a touch, something like that, will pick the baby up again; is that your experience?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And was that tried in the first instance?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Was that successful or not?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: So what was the next stage if there was one?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Facial oxygen.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: All right. Who administered facial oxygen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Lucy.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Where would that oxygen be obtained from?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's in the wall by each cot space.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And how would it look to a layperson like me if it was being administered?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So it's just a facial mask that goes over the baby's nose and mouth.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Did the baby respond to the help with the oxygen?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not at first, no.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. So did the saturations continue to fall or did they just remain at a low level?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I can't remember what they were.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: What happened to the alarm?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. Tell us what happened next then, please, when the baby didn't immediately respond to the additional oxygen.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: So then I think I saw a nurse walk past, Kate, so I shouted for help again.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Kate who?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Bissell.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. Where was Kate Bissell?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was on the unit, just walking past the door.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Any reason why you asked for help?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because the baby wasn't picking up.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Is that something you would ordinarily do?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Shout for help? I shout for help all the time, yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Right, okay. Did Ms Bissell respond?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She did, yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Anybody else?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I think there was a doctor sat outside on the computer, who came as well.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Do you remember the doctor's name at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: All right. Tell us, please, what happened when Ms Bissell and the doctor came in?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The oxygen obviously then was working, gentle stimulation was given, and then the baby recovered.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. Are you able to say how long it took before the baby recovered?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't know.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Once the baby had recovered, what happened then?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: The doctor and Kate had left the room and then basically -- not shouted at, but Lucy had said, "Why did you shout for help?" To me enough help -- you can't have enough help.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: She asked you why you shouted for help. In what way did she ask you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Quite firmly.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: How did you feel about that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Shocked.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Why?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because you can't have enough help in that situation.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. Did you explain to her why you asked for help?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't think I did, no.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Why not?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because you trust your colleagues, don't you?
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. How did you feel when she said this to you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Quite taken aback and shocked.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Why?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because it's something you wouldn't think a nurse would say, "Why are you shouting for help?", if you clearly need it.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: What was her demeanour when she was talking to you?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: She was quite firm.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. You can't remember the name of the baby or the doctor, but is there any reason why it sticks in your memory?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: It's because I was told off for shouting for help.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. Did you ever discuss it with her again?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: What would you expect -- in your experience what would other members of staff have done in such circumstances?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: They would have done the same.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Thank you. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
I don't know if it's Ms Walker or Mrs Walker?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Ms Walker is fine.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Ms Walker, I'm just going to ask you a couple of questions, not a great deal. You've told us about two incidents. One of them involved [Baby D] and a doctor.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: The other one involved a baby that Lucy Letby was looking after, who isn't [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: I just want to ask you about that one first, then I'll ask you about the other one. The one involving Lucy Letby, you're not sure when that happened. I'm not criticising you for that, but you're just not sure?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: You don't know the name of the child --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: -- is that right? You don't remember the sex of the child?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And just so we're quite clear, so no one misunderstands, you didn't see anything with regard to Ms Letby's actions or treatment of the baby that caused you any concern at all, did you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not at all, no.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: No, not at all, all right. She'd been feeding the baby as you'd been feeding another baby; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And you became aware, because the monitor sounded, that the oxygen level had fallen to some extent; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: I think you know in your experience, Ms Walker, it's not actually unusual for the oxygen level to fall when a baby's being fed, is it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Not at all.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: That happens. And you saw Ms Letby stop the feed. I'm just checking that's right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: She gave gentle stimulation, which is what you'd expect at first and then, when that didn't seem to work, she then gave the baby some oxygen; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: It's about that point when you called Kate Bissell to come and help?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And Kate Bissell and a doctor came in; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And I think in fact, although they came in, by that point nobody really needed to do anything because the oxygen levels had increased?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: All right, thanks. But as you've told us, afterwards there was a discussion from Ms Letby as to why you thought you needed to call for help?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And did -- the impression that you got was that she wasn't so much annoyed as she was just thinking that she didn't need any help?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't take it like that. She was cross that I shouted for help.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. I think you told the police:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Lucy's demeanour when she said to me what she did wasn't really being annoyed, I don't think, I think it was saying she would have been fine and didn't need any help."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what you told the police.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: All right. Anyway, the baby was fine?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: All right. That involves a baby that we're not concerned with here in this case.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask you about [Baby D], who is a baby that we are concerned with. You saw [Baby D] on the time she was being brought into the neonatal unit; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And you saw that she looked blue in colour?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And you saw that the doctor who she was with didn't appear to be responding at all to that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Now, that is something that you were unhappy about when you witnessed that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: You took the cot and you called for help, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And then [Nurse A ] came and took [Baby D] into the nursery, where she was put into an incubator?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And you have a system, don't you, at the hospital where if you see a matter that causes concern, you can report that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: And that's called the Datix system; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: So given what you saw on that occasion with that doctor and [Baby D], you did make a report of that on Datix, didn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I did.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: Okay. That's all I wanted to ask, Ms Walker.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have nothing further.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Does my Lord have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Questions from THE JUDGE
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just this. The incident that involved Lucy Letby, you can't remember when it was --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: -- in relation to this earlier incident concerning [Baby D]? Can you remember whether it was a night shift or a day shift?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It was a day shift.
blocks.speaker: WALKER

blocks.text: It was a day shift, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. That completes your evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you for coming and giving it. This witness isn't giving evidence again?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'll check, but I don't think so. No.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: You won't be required to come and give evidence again, so thank you very much for coming and giving evidence this afternoon. Please don't talk to anyone who knows anything about this case until it's all over.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: All right? Thank you very much. If you just wait there for the moment.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, I'm afraid that's as far as we can go today, for reasons that I think my Lord knows about with the next witness.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: All right. Yes, we can't take it any further this afternoon, the evidence. We'd have to have a break in any event. 10.30 tomorrow, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you very much indeed.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

I'm going to rise now. You just stay where you are until you're told to move, all right?

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
